G-Power-Tuned BMW 8 Series Offers 620 Reasons To Love It, Taps Out at 186 MPH
6 photos
Photo: Instagram | gpower_world
The BMW 8 Series may be no more, just like its top flavor, the M8, but while production may have officially ceased earlier this year, this model remains in our hearts as being one of the best-looking Bimmers in the company’s recent history.
And it’s not only in our hearts, because it also continues to live in quite a few circles, including the tuning one, and we haven’t mentioned it for nothing, because G-Power recently shared the above images in a social media post, while also revealing a few things about the project in question, which not only looks more aggressive, but also has more than enough power for daily drives and not only.
According to the tuner, this BMW M850i is equipped with the GP-620 bundle, and as you can imagine, it has 620 horsepower. That’s metric horsepower, which equals to 612 brake horsepower and 456 kilowatts. The peak output has increased to 627 pound-feet (850 Nm). The car is said to be capable of reaching 186 mph (300 kph) flat out, and it is not even the most extreme offering from G-Power for this model.
That one would be the GP-670, which, as its name implies, brings 661 hp (670 ps/493 kW) to the party and 664 pound-feet (900 Nm) of torque. In this case, you must fork out 13,014.99 euros (equal to $14,575) for the bundle, whereas the GP-620 will set you back a more down-to-earth 2,495 euros ($2,795) on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.
Photo: Instagram | gpower_world By comparison, the stock BMW M850i has 523 hp (530 ps/390 kW) and 553 (750 Nm) of torque to play with. The twin-turbocharged 4.4-liter V8 engine rockets it to 62 mph (100 kph) in just 3.7 seconds. We would love to tell you how fast the model is with the GP-620 and the GP-670 upgrades. However, G-Power hasn’t released this information at the time of writing.
Nevertheless, the time has likely dropped to less than 3.5 seconds. After all, the M8 had 591 hp (600 ps/441 kW) and 553 lb-ft (750 Nm) of torque to play with, and completed the sprint in 3.3 seconds. The M8 Competition boosted the output to 617 hp (625 ps/460 kW), retaining the same thrust, and it was one-tenth of a second faster than the non-Competition model.
As for the Alpina B8 , which was also a thing until earlier this year, it zipped from 0-62 mph in 3.3 seconds, aided by the 612 hp (620 ps/456 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque produced by its tuned 4.4-liter twin-turbo V8, which was shared with the M850i xDrive.
The pictured 8er also benefits from a few other upgrades from the same tuner, such as the Venturi carbon fiber hood, GP-Dynamic carbon fiber rear wing, and a set of Hurricane RS 21-inch forged wheels. The rear silencer with four carbon tailpipes is also part of the makeover. The tuner also offers a splitter, side flaps, a new steering wheel, aftermarket paddle shifters, velour floor mats, and even a complete interior makeover for this model, as well as a coil-over spring set and numerous other wheel options.
Photo: Instagram | gpower_world By the way, these also fit other 8ers, not only the M850i , and for the lesser 840i, G-Power also offers two powertrain upgrades. The superior version is called the GP-450. It has 444 hp (450 ps/331 kW) and 457 lb-ft (620 Nm) of torque, costing 4,932 euros ($5,523), and the GP-400 has 395 hp (400 ps/294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm) of torque, and will cost you 1,995 euros ($2,235).
BMW’s standard 840i and 840i xDrive had 335 hp (340 ps/250 kW) and 332 pound-feet (450 Nm) of torque to play with, with power being supplied by the B58 engine, a 3.0-liter turbocharged straight-six unit. The RWD model hit 62 mph (100 kph) in 5.3 seconds, and the rear-biased all-wheel drive version completed the acceleration in 4.9 seconds.
So, there you have it, ladies and gents, another cool project from G-Power that;s bound to turn heads wherever it goes. The power boost is definitely a great upgrade for this model, and I reckon, with an emphasis on “I,” that the wheels and sport suspension are nice touches. I’m not entirely convinced that the carbon hood and rear wing suit the nature of this ride, nor its overall design to be honest, but hey, at least it’s not a kitschy build.
Far from it, actually, as G-Power can easily host a car-tuning game, as other companies could learn a thing or two. Now, if you owned a G1X BMW 8 Series, would you turn to G-Power for more oomph? By the way, the tuner’s portfolio also includes power upgrades and other bits and bobs for the entire M8 lineup, too, which comprises the same body styles, namely a coupe, a convertible, and a sedan (Gran Coupe), in case you forgot. Time Capsule 1969 Impala SS 427 Has Every Factory Option, No One Cares About It
21 photos
Photo: fFcebook Marketplace/Taylor McMillian
For Chevrolet enthusiasts, 1969 was a dramatic year of lasts: it was the last year for the Super Sport Impala, the last year for the 427-cubic-inch V8 big-block, the last year for the ferocious Corvette L88, and the last year for the first-generation Camaro. So how in the world can one of the rarest Impalas ever made sit for 5 weeks unnoticed, still waiting for someone brave enough to take it home?
Hiding in plain sight in St. Joseph, Missouri, just 30 minutes from Kansas City International Airport, this 1969 Chevrolet Impala Custom Coupe carries an asking price of $47,500 and shows a mere 36,000 original miles on the clock. Bearing Vehicle Identification Number 164479S037467, the big-block cruiser rolled off the St. Louis, Missouri assembly line during the second week of February 1969 as a General Motors executive-ordered brass-hat car for the Chevrolet Motor Division.
Apparently, Detroit brass knew how to check every worthwhile box on an order sheet before handing the keys over to Kizzier Chevrolet in Scottsbluff, Nebraska, on May 23, 1969. After serving its executive tour of duty, the dealership sold the coupe on August 29, 1969, to Jake Rein of Gering, Nebraska. The original window sticker shows a $3,068.00 base price, a $124.50 destination fee, and $1,829.00 in options, totaling $5,021.50.
Dressed in Azure Turquoise under a $100.10 white vinyl roof with parchment and black vinyl trim, this highway land yacht packed $168.55 Strato-Bucket front seats, a console, $384.45 4-Season air conditioning, a $221.80 Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 transmission, and the $422.35 Z24 SS 427 package. It also added a $133.80 8-track player, $61.10 AM radio, $105.35 power steering, $45.30 tilt wheel, $77.05 G70-15 redline tires, and $26.35 fiber-optic lights monitoring.
Photo: fFcebook Marketplace/Taylor McMillian Rounding out the sticker were $42.15 Soft-Ray tinted glass, $16.90 head restraints, $12.15 deluxe seat and shoulder belts, and $11.60 floor mats. Its Protect-O-Plate verifies the Tonawanda-built 390-hp 427 V8, the automatic transmission, and the 2.73:1 ratio in the 12-bolt rear axle. When the original block developed a thirst for oil in the early 1970s, Kizzier Chevrolet installed a factory CE warranty short block, retaining al l original components.
Aside from a minor lower passenger fender repair, a fresh coat of Azure Turquoise paint, new seat upholstery, replacement carpet, and Coker GR70-15 redline radial tires wrapped around 15-inch YZ steel wheels with poverty caps, the car remains a time-capsule survivor. Original floor pans, trunk spatter, T3 headlights, vinyl top, door panels, and a YZ spare wheel are still there.
To appreciate this turquoise Super Sport, we ought to look back at the Impala lineage, which began in 1958 as a top-tier Bel Air package that seduced roughly 60,000 buyers across convertible and hardtop models. Promoted to a standalone series in 1959, the Impala ruled American highways continuously until 1985, briefly returned as an iron-fisted performance sedan from 1994 to 1996, and served as a mainstream sedan from 2000 to 2020.
Photo: fFcebook Marketplace/Taylor McMillian Things got spicier in 1961 when Chevrolet introduced the Impala Super Sport, or SS, as a genuine muscle package that found just 453 takers, including 142 with the 409-cubic-inch V8. Once Chevrolet opened the SS trim to all engines, sales exploded to 99,311 cars in 1962, 153,271 in 1963, and 185,325 in 1964, before peaking at 243,114 in 1965 and sliding to 119,314 in 1966, 76,055 in 1967, and 38,210 in 1968.
For its 1969 swan song, Chevrolet restored the Super Sport to pure muscle status by merging the Impala SS exclusively into the RPO Z24 SS 427 package. Out of 777,000 total Impalas built for 1969, including 768,000 V8 cars and 8,700 6-cylinder models, both Impala SS and Impala SS 427 production stood at a mere 2,455 units, making this Missouri hardtop rarer than plenty of $100,000 midsize Chevelle Super Sports.
Between 1961 and 1968, buyers could order an Impala SS with everything from thrifty 235-cubic-inch and 250-cubic-inch inline-six engines or 283, 307, and 327 small-block V8s to 348 and 409 W-blocks, the 1963 Z11 427, and 396 or 427 Mark IV big-blocks. In 1969, however, Chevrolet banished small-blocks and 6-cylinders from the SS, offering only 427 cubic inches in the Super Sport rated at 390 hp or 425 hp inside the Z24 package.
Photo: fFcebook Marketplace/Taylor McMillian Debuting in 1967 with 2,124 built and continuing in 1968 with 1,778 examples, RPO Z24 originally brought a domed hood, heavy-duty suspension, dual exhausts, and special badging to full-size Chevrolets. For its 1969 finale, the $422.35 Z24 package bundled the biggest Chevrolet motor, bright engine accents, standard power front disc brakes, heavy-duty 15x6-inch steel wheels, G70-15 wide-oval tires, upgraded chassis, a black-accented grille, simulated fender louvers, and “SS 427” badges.
Under the hood, the base L36 427-cubic-inch V8 featured a 10.25:1 compression, and a Quadrajet carburetor to deliver 390 hp at 4,800 rpm and 460 lb-ft of torque (624 Nm) at 3,200 rpm. Even weighed down by full-size prestige , an automatic 1969 Impala SS 427 tested by Car Life magazine sprinted from 0 to 60 mph in 8.4 seconds and cleared the 1,320-foot run in 15.75 seconds at 86.5 mph.
The alternative to that 427 was the L72 big-bore powerhouse, with solid lifters, 11.0:1 compression, a Holley four-throater, and 425 hp. Torque stayed at the same 460 lb-ft. The example in the gallery has left that option out – probably because GM decided the public didn’t need to know about.
Photo: fFcebook Marketplace/Taylor McMillian No advertising promotions, no mention of this motor in any of the promotional and sales materials, and unless you were sharp with the order form, you probably didn’t even know you could get such a thing in 1969, because Chevy certainly wasn’t talking about it.
A total of 546 L72 engines were built and they were installed in a variety of Chevy vehicles (they were not exclusive to the Impala, you could get it in your Kingswood station wagon if you were savvy), making them quite rare.
Stacking the $47,500 asking price against public auction results over the past five years makes the hesitation of collectors even funnier. On Bring a Trailer, a 62,000-mile L36 SS 427 coupe brought $50,000 in August 2021, while a modified convertible fetched $45,000 in January 2023, and Mecum and Barrett-Jackson examples commanded between $44,000 and $66,000. For a documented 36,000-mile brass-hat survivor, $47,500 is an absolute bargain hiding in St. Joseph, Missouri.

BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology.
BYD debuts new Cloud Carriage body control system
BYD launched the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the new choice for a class-leading luxury experience.”
It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.
Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.
The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).
Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.
The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.
The setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.
Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.
BYD said the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm.
It’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get.
Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.
BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio.
The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely.
Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.
For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a big catch.
Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to new data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence . That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.
Region | Oct-26, million | y-o-y | m-o-m | YTD, millions | YTD-26 vs YTD-25
China | 1.14 | -12% | 5% | 9.1 | -11%
Europe | 0.51 | 36% | -17% | 4.5 | 31%
North America | 0.13 | 24% | 0% | 1.3 | -21%
RoW | 0.30 | 85% | -2% | 2.6 | 93%
Global | 2.09 | 8% | -3% | 17.5 | 5%
Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
Europe’s growth keeps building
Europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.
Sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.
Germany’s EV share topped 45% of new car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.
UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.
And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of new car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.
North America’s rebound needs context
North American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.
US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.
But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.
October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.
“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” said Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.
The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.
China sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.
Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.
Even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s new car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.
Chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of new energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.
Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.
Other markets grow fast, with some caveats
Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.
Australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.
Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.
As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

Trystar, LLC is introducing five (5) new series of relays in a narrow 17.5mm wide DIN-rail form factor, with dedicated solutions for timing, load alternation, and voltage and phase monitoring. Designed for OEMs, panel builders, and industrial users (including water/wastewater management, automation, HVAC, refrigeration, petrochemical, and agriculture), this new portfolio of compact relays helps conserve valuable panel space while providing purpose-built solutions for timing control, equipment protection, voltage monitoring, and load management.
As control panels are expected to accommodate more functionality in an increasingly limited space, the narrow 17.5mm design enables greater component density and additional flexibility in enclosure planning. A consistent form factor across the entire series also simplifies panel layouts, and makes it easier for customers to select the appropriate relay functionality for each of their applications. Across the portfolio, these new relays provide additional features such as industrial-grade construction, integration with common control devices (e.g., contactors, motor starters, and PLC inputs), and visible status indication. Depending upon the series, available capabilities also include adjustable timing, universal control voltages, sequence control, adjustable monitoring thresholds, and field-selectable functions.
Trystar’s new 17.5mm relay portfolio includes:
TE5 Series – Time Delay Relays: Straightforward, precise time-based control through a dedicated function and time range, eliminating complicated setup.
TE6 Series – Multifunction Timing Relays: Combining multiple timing ranges and selectable functions in one device to give OEMs and panel builders greater application flexibility.
PxE Series – 3-Phase Monitoring and Protection Relays: Continuously monitor 3-phase power for potentially damaging conditions; including phase loss, reversal, and imbalance, as well as over- and under-voltage conditions.
AE-1 Series – Alternating Relays: Automatically alternate operation between two loads such as pumps, compressors, or fans; which extends equipment life and improves overall system availability.
VxE Series – 1-Phase Voltage Monitoring Relays: Continuously check and adjust AC or DC power quality for over- and under-voltage conditions.
Panel designers need compact components, but they also need the flexibility to address very different control and equipment-protection requirements. This new portfolio brings five (5) distinct relay series together in one space-efficient form factor, giving customers a straightforward way to add the functionality their application requires.

Financial distress continues to ripple through the U.S. transportation and logistics industry, with more than 1,000 announced job cuts and a new round of bankruptcy filings involving trucking companies , warehouse operators and freight-related businesses .
At least 10 companies have disclosed plans to eliminate a combined 1,021 jobs, according to layoff announcements and Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) notices compiled by FreightWaves between late October and Nov. 11.
The reductions affect workers in California, Ohio, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Connecticut and New York, with several warehouse closures and layoffs scheduled to take effect in early 2027.
Meanwhile, 15 transportation, distribution and freight-related businesses have filed for Chapter 7 liquidation or Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in cases dated between Sept. 14 and Nov. 10, including 13 filings since Oct. 19.
Warehouse and logistics layoffs account for hundreds of jobs
Among the largest announced reductions is DSV Contract Logistics LLC, which plans to eliminate 175 jobs at its Edwardsville, Illinois, facility beginning Dec. 5.
According to an Illinois WARN notice, the permanent layoffs at the company’s Illinois facility are tied to a lost contract.
National Distribution Centers LLC also announced significant workforce reductions at two facilities.
The company plans to close its distribution facility in Perris, California, eliminating 167 jobs effective Jan. 4, 2027. In Groveport, Ohio, the company intends to permanently eliminate another 126 positions between Jan. 5 and Jan. 19.
Combined, the two actions account for 293 announced job cuts.
Other logistics companies announcing reductions include CEVA Supply Chain Inc., which plans to eliminate 120 positions at its Lockbourne, Ohio, facility by June 2027, and Kenco Logistic Services LLC, which is permanently closing a warehouse operation near Myerstown, Pennsylvania.
Kenco’s closure will affect 81 employees, with layoffs beginning March 1 and concluding by June 15.
Worldwide Flight Services Inc., an air cargo handling and ground services provider, filed an Oct. 29 WARN notice covering 59 permanent layoffs at its San Diego facility.
Amazon also announced plans Nov. 9 to close its La Puente fulfillment center in Southern California, affecting 94 employees at the end of January. Some employees may be eligible to transfer to other Amazon locations.
The reductions extend beyond warehouses and distribution centers.
Oshkosh Corp. eliminated approximately 80 salaried positions in its transport segment in late October. The cuts coincided with the specialty vehicle manufacturer’s third-quarter earnings announcement, when it lowered its full-year profit outlook.
S&S Worldwide, a Connecticut-based distributor of crafts and educational supplies, announced 70 layoffs, while S.S. Delivery Systems LLC filed a facility closure notice affecting 49 workers in Rochester, New York.

Several carriers filed for Chapter 7 liquidation, including Winners Trucking Inc. of Dallas, Texas; Bruin Logistics LLC of Cicero, Illinois; and JYM Trucking Inc. of Florida.
Winners Trucking filed its voluntary Chapter 7 petition Oct. 21 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of Texas. The case was designated a no-asset proceeding.
Bruin Logistics filed a Chapter 7 petition Nov. 9 in the Northern District of Illinois, also designated as a no-asset case.
JYM Trucking, a carrier listed with one truck and one driver, filed for Chapter 7 protection Oct. 27 in the Middle District of Florida.
Other Chapter 7 filings included RP3 Hauler Inc., an Orlando-based auto transport and interstate freight carrier, and Priority Freight & Logistics Corp., which filed in Pennsylvania.
Chapter 7 generally involves liquidating a company’s nonexempt assets to satisfy creditor claims, while Chapter 11 allows a business to reorganize its debts or pursue other court-supervised restructuring options.
Texas trucking and repair companies pursue restructuring
Several Texas transportation businesses have sought Chapter 11 protection.
X-Total Cattle Transportation LLC, an El Paso-based livestock carrier, filed Nov. 10 in the Western District of Texas.
The company reported liabilities between $500,000 and $1 million, compared with assets of less than $50,000.
Federal transportation records cited in the filing summary show the company previously operated four power units and employed five drivers. Its USDOT registration was listed as inactive as of October.
Tri State Truck Repair LLC, also based in El Paso, filed for Chapter 11 protection Nov. 2, reporting assets and liabilities each between $500,000 and $1 million.
The company provides heavy-duty truck repair and maintenance services along the Interstate 10 corridor.
SW Truck Care LLC, a commercial truck repair and inspection business in Grand Prairie, Texas, filed for Chapter 11 protection Nov. 9. The company reported assets and liabilities each between $1 million and $10 million.
In Florida, KR Transport & Services LLC, an agricultural hauling business, filed for Chapter 11 protection Oct. 29, reporting assets and liabilities between $1 million and $10 million.
Supply chain bankruptcies extend beyond trucking
Financial distress is also affecting companies involved in freight distribution, automotive parts and agricultural supply chains.
Grapeman LLC, a California-based fresh fruit distributor, filed for Chapter 11 protection Oct. 23, reporting liabilities between $10 million and $50 million against assets of $1 million to $10 million.
Getpart LA Inc., an automotive collision parts e-commerce retailer operating under the Fitparts brand, filed for Chapter 11 protection Oct. 26.
The Gardena, California-based company operates a national distribution network supporting automotive parts sales.
Torres Metal Recycling Inc., a Sealy, Texas-based industrial recycling business, also filed for Chapter 11 protection Oct. 23.

This 1990 Ford F-150 by Roush Was Sold Back in September. Now It Hits the Market Again
39 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
This Roush 1990 Ford F-150 Concept Sport Truck was kept safely inside the private Roush Family Collection from the day it was built until earlier this fall. Since then, it has already hit the auction block twice. It looks like it's living a life in the spotlight after over three decades of storage.
Meet the Roush -built 1990 Ford F-150 Concept Sport Truck. Again. You have probably seen it before back in September, when it was auctioned off at the Mecum Nashville auction. Back then, it fetched $41,800. Now, the one who paid for it has already listed it for sale.
The Roush F-150 comes from an era when factory-backed sport trucks like the SVT Lightning or the GMC Syclone had not yet hit the market. Roush Industries built only two signature concept sport trucks. Both were designed as rolling promotional billboards for trackside events, sponsor tie-ins, and to showcase the company’s expanding engineering catalog.
What you are looking at is Truck #1, the so-called Valvoline Truck. It is powered by a 351-cubic-inch (5.8-liter) V8 engine, and it is finished in a white, red, and blue paint scheme, mimicking NASCAR legend Mark Martin's No. 6 Valvoline Ford Thunderbird. Martin drove it to 15 NASCAR Cup Series victories.
Photo: Bring a Trailer As for Truck #2, The Family Channel Truck, it was built slightly later to celebrate Roush's mid-1990s partnership with The Family Channel. The sibling of the Valvoline Truck featured a radically different powertrain setup. It came with a monstrous 525-cubic-inch V8 under the hood, pushing out 450 horsepower (456 metric horsepower). This truck also sold in Nashville back in September for $29,700.
But only the Valvoline Truck is back on the market, the second time in two months. This time, the seller is Bullet Motorsport, a dealership specializing in niche market car sales, transport, consignment, and storage. Now, the truck they acquired back in September is already looking for its next collection, where it will probably spend time untouched, because that is what collector vehicles do.
Under the hood, the Windsor V8 with naturally aspirated firepower makes 375 horsepower (380 metric horsepower), says the seller, even though there is no dyno sheet or official factory rating. Back in the day, the standard 5.8-liter V8 was good for 210 horsepower (213 metric horsepower) before being dialed up by Roush Industries.
Roush achieved that sort of oomph by installing Trick Flow Specialties (TFS) aluminum cylinder heads, Crane aluminum roller rocker arms, high-rate Crane valve springs, and a Crane hydraulic roller camshaft. The V8 is fed by custom Roush-engineered intake track-focused components and exhales through a bespoke sport-tone dual exhaust system integrated with catalytic converters.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Unlike the typical auto-box trucks of the era, the Valvoline Truck comes with a T5OD five-speed manual transmission, complete with a low-inertia clutch/flywheel assembly and a rugged scatter-shield bellhousing. The setup puts the power down through the rear wheels. The truck sits on an 8.8-inch rear end with factory 3.55:1 limited-slip gears.
Roush tweaked the truck’s Twin I-Beam front suspension and slammed it to the ground for more drama. The firm completely discarded the factory rear drums in favor of a modern four-wheel disc brake conversion. The truck sits on aggressively styled, period-correct 17×9.5″ Center Line modular wheels wrapped in massive 315/35 Goodyear Eagle GS-C tires at all four corners.
This truck started out in life as a standard eighth-gen F-150 XLT Lariat 4x2 short-bed, the so-called Bricknose generation. Roush retrofitted it with a Flareside bed box, rocker moldings, an integrated roll pan, and custom grab handles, mounted just above the sliding rear glass window.
The blue interior features high-bolstered factory sport bucket seats originally sourced from a 1991 Ford Ranger, a customized center console, a full padded roll cage, and Simpson cam-lock racing harnesses to secure the driver and passenger in place.
Photo: Bring a Trailer Roush also came up with a premium Ford AM/FM radio using all-OEM components. The Grant GT steering wheel frames a speedometer scaled up to 180 mph (290 kph), flanked by auxiliary gauges and a 9,000 rpm tachometer.
With 12,403 original miles (19,961 kilometers) on the odometer, traveled in 36 years, the truck is still a time capsule, but carries a few minor quirks, which are nothing out of the ordinary considering the vehicle’s age. There are blemishes on the front bumper and small paint imperfections. The air conditioning was just fully serviced with fresh refrigerant by the selling dealer, but they mention there is a finicky radio button with a mind of its own.
Whoever takes this baby home will also get the original Roush build sheet, owner's manuals, a clean Carfax report with the odometer reading listed as “Exempt” due to the truck’s age, a clean Montana title, and a piece of memorabilia: an authentic red racing glove.
With two days to go, the most generous offer on Bring a Trailer so far has just hit $30,006. The dealer is probably trying to cash in and will by no means let it go for anything less than what they paid for the truck back in September.

Father painted this 1955 Chevy Bel Air in 1972, then parked it for 30 years. His son drives it again
15 photos
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube
Three young men took on an incredible project back in the early 1970s: to build the ultimate 1955 Chevrolet Bel Air show car. They went around Canada winning awards for a while, but then, its owner parked it and hardly ever touched it in the next 30 years. Now, his son travels around America in it, stealing the show everywhere he goes.
Gary Ponich is the son of the man who came up with the idea of converting his 1955 Chevrolet Bel Air into a show car that would turn heads and win awards. He built this car alongside two buddies back in 1972. They were all in their early 20s, all students at art school.
Gary’s father was the one who sprayed it silver. When he was done, he handed a box of candy paint to his buddies, and this is what came out of their hands. Bruce did the mural on the back, showing a red Bel Air cruising down the coast, and the atomic bomb on the roof. They originally planned to make it an all-red car, but they got creative along the way.
It took them 16 months to complete the car, using House of Kolor lacquer. They started on the left side front corner with plenty of enthusiasm and meticulous drawing and painting, but they gradually lost it along the way, so that the right side ended up displaying only waves in blue and red.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube It interior, Gary has always called Waffle House, as he had no idea what wrapped the seats, headliner, dashboard, and the door panels until recently. One day, an older gentleman walked up to him and told him it was called “Statesman,” available in five colors (gold, silver, blue, red, and green) in the 1960s and early 1970s.
The trio drove it across Canada and the United States and made plans about taking it overseas one day. But that day never came for him. His friend, Bruce, still visits every once in a while, bringing stories from their early 20s.
For instance, he recalls how, after completing the car in 1972, they took it to a car show, hoping to win the Best Engine Compartment Award. They gloriously failed, so they went home, rebuilt everything in the engine bay from scratch, and two years later, at another car show, they won the award for the Best Engine Compartment and every award available.
At some point, the car simply disappeared from the public eye as Gary’s father had to deal with health issues. In the meantime, he passed away, and his son felt he had to carry on his legacy. So he pulled the car out of storage, had it up and running, and started doing what his father used to do: going to car shows and winning awards.
Photo: Magnacars | YouTube The colors have faded over the years, especially during the past year, when the car traveled a lot. It was no longer a car parked in the family garage. It was again the show car it was built to be. One day, while driving to a car show, he had a close encounter with a deer, and the Chevy Bel Air was left with severe battle scars.
But a few friends, including Bruce, jumped in to help and, by the end of the week, everything was straight back again, in time for another car show in Sacramento. He came home with one more trophy. But it is not just about the trophy for him. It is about the attention and the smiles he gets everywhere he goes.
The most impressive story is meeting a gentleman in California who remembered he had seen the exact same Bel Air in British Columbia, Canada, when he was 12. He immediately snapped a photo and sent it to his brother because they had been talking about the unforgettable Bel Air that they had seen when they were just kids.
What powers the 1955 Bel Air is a 283-cubic-inch V8 swapped from a 1957 Chevrolet, while an M21 four-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels. Back in 1957, the 283 V8 came in four distinct flavors, with the base engine making 185 horsepower (189 metric horsepower), while the range-topping variant with a Rochester mechanical fuel injection boasted 283 horsepower (287 metric horsepower).
{fulimg9}
Rather than treating his father's coupe as the ultimate garage queen, Gary Ponich has logged roughly 11,000 miles (17,703 kilometers) on the odometer in 2026 alone. The Chevy Bel Air has become not only Gary's pride and joy, but also his daily driver.
He has recently downsized his car collection and only kept the Bel Air and the Caprice . He doesn't need a new car. He doesn’t need all the creature comforts of a modern vehicle. He doesn't even need navigation, because for him, it is always about the journey, not the destination. Besides, you know what they say: life is too short to drive boring cars.
Gary told his story to TJ Lamb of Magnacars.

For three and a half years the smallest tier of trucking has been quietly emptying out, with the number of tractors run by one-to-six-truck carriers sliding from a 2023 peak near 398,000 all the way back to about 362,000, and the easy explanation, that owner-operators are simply going out of business, misses what the federal data actually shows, because a large share of those trucks never leave the road at all, they just change whose name is on the authority . The story of the shrinking owner-operator tier is really two stories, one about why they are getting squeezed out and one about where the equipment lands, and the second one is the more interesting of the two.
The Exodus, By The Numbers
The scale of the retreat is clear in the fleet-size data. FreightWaves SONAR’s count of tractors operated by carriers with one to six power units (TCTCO.USA) sits at 362,033, below both its five-year average of about 378,800 and its 12-month average of roughly 364,960. The segment surged during the freight boom, as pandemic-era demand and easy authority pulled a wave of new entrants into the market, peaked close to 398,000 tractors in the first half of 2023, and has declined almost without interruption since . That is roughly 36,000 tractors, on the order of nine percent of the segment, pulled back out of the smallest tier over three and a half years, effectively unwinding the entire boom.
What makes that remarkable is how many operators the tier still holds. In the latest FMCSA census , more than 1.8 million active carrier registrations fall into the one-to-six-truck band, a count that includes private and intrastate operators alongside for-hire freight haulers, and it is the overwhelming majority of all registered carriers. This is not a small corner of trucking thinning out, it is the broadest base of the market contracting at the edges, and it has been doing so steadily regardless of which way freight has moved month to month.
The Squeeze, Starting With Fuel
The reasons owner-operators are leaving are not mysterious, they are mathematical, and they come from both sides of the ledger at once. On the cost side, running a truck set a record in 2025, with the American Transportation Research Institute putting the average marginal cost at 2.336 dollars per mile. In that 2025 breakdown, driver pay was the heaviest line at roughly 82 cents per mile, with fuel the next tier down at about 48 cents. Then 2026 rewrote the fuel math entirely. Diesel set records this year , with the Department of Energy’s national on-highway average topping its previous all-time high in September and reaching 6.127 dollars a gallon by the week of November 9 .
At the six to seven miles per gallon a working truck gets, diesel over six dollars a gallon runs roughly a dollar a mile in fuel alone, close to double what fuel cost a year earlier, and that increase landed on top of a cost base that was already the highest ATRI had ever recorded. The run-up was not purely a refining story, crude oil climbed back above 100 dollars a barrel in the same stretch, but diesel outran crude as global refining capacity tightened. For the operator trying to pencil out a load, a cost that used to be the second or third line on the sheet is now vying to be the biggest.
For the owner-operator, that dollar-a-mile fuel hit is close to unavoidable, because most small carriers never get the benefit of a fuel surcharge in the first place. A surcharge is largely a contract-freight mechanism, a separate line that moves with the Department of Energy’s weekly diesel average and shows up on dedicated and committed lanes. The small operator living on load-board freight from the spot market rarely sees one, because spot rates are quoted all-in, a single number that already bakes in whatever the broker is willing to pay that day. There is no surcharge line to adjust when diesel spikes, so the owner-operator absorbs the full move into a rate they never got to reprice. A mid-sized fleet running contract freight under a negotiated surcharge program recovers a chunk of every fuel increase, while the spot-dependent owner-operator recovers almost none of it. The same gallon costs them more and comes back to them less.
Insurance is the other cost that lands hardest on the smallest. Premiums ran around 10.6 cents per mile in 2025, up nearly four percent on the year and well above where they sat just a few years ago, and the operator with one or two trucks pays the most per unit with the least ability to self-insure or negotiate. Stack record fuel, rising insurance, and the fastest increases ATRI tracked in tolls, maintenance, and driver benefits on top of each other, and the structural problem is simple, there is no scale to spread any of it across.
The Other Jaw Of The Vise, Costs Outrunning Rates
Here is the part that gets misread. Rates are not the owner-operator’s problem the way they were a couple of years ago. Spot van and reefer rates have firmed through 2026, running stronger for this time of year than any season since 2021, and contract pricing is forecast to climb meaningfully into next year, with some dry-van estimates calling for double-digit increases. Freight volume, for its part, has stayed roughly flat rather than surging, with the SONAR Truckload Volume Index ( STVI.USA ) holding near its average instead of breaking higher.
So the squeeze on the small operator is not that rates are falling, it is that costs are rising faster than rates can keep up, and the single biggest of those costs, fuel, is the one a spot carrier has no surcharge to recover. A mid-sized fleet hauling contract freight captures the rising rate and claws back fuel through a surcharge program at the same time. The owner-operator on the load board captures the better rate but eats the full fuel increase underneath it, so even a firming market leaves them with thinner net than the headline number suggests. Put the two sides together and the picture is a margin vise, fuel and insurance climbing faster than even a rising rate can cover for a carrier with no surcharge and no scale, and the thinner the cushion, the faster it closes. For a lot of these operators, leaving does not mean parking the truck and walking away from the industry. It means making a rational business decision about where that truck can earn a living, and increasingly the answer is not under their own authority.
Where The Trucks Go, Part One
Here is where the federal data gets genuinely revealing. Pull the FMCSA census and break out, for each fleet-size band, the share of a carrier’s tractors that are leased rather than owned, and a clean pattern appears. Owner-operators run almost entirely owned equipment, with only about 6.9 percent of their tractors leased. Move up to small fleets of seven to 19 trucks and the leased share jumps to 18.2 percent. By the mid-sized band of 20 to 100 trucks, nearly a third of all tractors, 31.6 percent, are leased rather than owned, and in the 101-to-999 band it climbs past 40 percent.
That rising curve is part of the mechanism of the migration, though it is worth being precise about what it captures. A leased tractor inside a larger fleet can be a former owner-operator who surrendered their own authority and leased on, bringing the truck with them, and it can also be equipment the fleet leases from a full-service lessor like Penske or Ryder. Both rise with fleet size, and both point the same direction, that larger fleets run a growing share of their capacity on trucks they do not own, which is exactly where owner-operators who give up their own authority tend to land. In the 20-to-100 band alone, the census shows more than 217,000 term-leased tractors sitting alongside roughly 466,000 owned ones, and that owned-tractor figure lines up closely with SONAR’s separate count of 470,402 tractors for the same band, a useful cross-check between two independent reads of the same market.
This is a big part of why the mid-sized segment keeps setting records while the smallest one shrinks. The 20-to-100 band is the natural landing spot for a capable operator who no longer wants to carry their own insurance, chase their own freight, and shoulder their own back-office load. The truck keeps rolling, the driver keeps driving, and the authority quietly changes hands.
Net changes in trucking authorities swung from a historic surge in 2020 and 2021 to years of net losses through 2022 and 2023 as carriers left the market, the same churn driving the owner-operator exodus. The recent jump to a net 1,279 is distorted by the FMCSA Motus rollout, which pushed a backlog of reinstatements through, so read it with caution. Source: FreightWaves SONAR (CDNCA.USA)
Where The Trucks Go, Part Two
Not every exiting owner-operator leases on. Some sell the truck outright, and that equipment does not leave the road either, it tends to get bought by fleets a size or two up that will take good used iron at a discount when smaller operators are offloading it. Whether through a lease-on or a sale, the trucks are consolidating into larger operations better built to run them profitably when fuel is this expensive.
Why The Middle Is Doing The Absorbing
The 20-to-100 tier is small in number but heavy in trucks. Only about 44,500 active carriers fall into that band, under two percent of all carriers, yet they operate roughly 1.75 million power units. They sit in the efficiency sweet spot, big enough to spread the rising cost of fuel, insurance, and equipment, and small enough to stay nimble and regional. A fleet in this band can negotiate a real fuel-surcharge program, buy diesel in volume, and spread insurance and maintenance across dozens of trucks, all things the lone owner-operator cannot. That is the cost advantage that lets the middle keep a truck earning when the same truck would lose money running on its own authority.
What It Means For The Operator Weighing The Move
For the owner-operator looking at their own segment in that long decline, the takeaway is not that the small carrier is doomed, it is that running small now demands more discipline than it used to. The operators holding their ground are the ones who know their true cost per mile to the penny, who built direct relationships with local shippers instead of depending on the spot market, and who run the truck like a business rather than a glorified job. The ones leasing on are frequently making the smart call, trading some independence for a cost structure and freight base they cannot build alone. The operators who end up surrendering their authority with nothing to show for it are usually the ones who drifted, undercapitalized and spot-dependent, until the fuel bills closed the math on them even as rates improved. The data cannot tell an individual which path to take, but it makes the stakes of the choice unmistakable.
Why It Matters
The steady shrinking of the one-to-six-truck tier is not a wave of trucks leaving the industry, it is a migration of equipment up the fleet-size ladder, squeezed out by record fuel and operating costs that climb faster than even a rising rate can cover for a spot carrier with no surcharge, and absorbed by mid-sized fleets through lease-ons and used-truck purchases, with the leased share of a fleet’s tractors climbing from under seven percent for owner-operators to nearly a third for the 20-to-100 band. For carriers, brokers, and shippers, that matters because the capacity base is quietly consolidating into larger, more durable operations that can withstand six-dollar diesel and flat volumes, which makes it stickier and harder to shake loose, and for the owner-operator specifically it reframes the central question of the moment, not whether to stay in trucking, but whether to stay in trucking alone.
This analysis draws on FreightWaves SONAR data for tractor counts by fleet size (TCTCO.USA at 362,033 and TCTCM.USA at 470,402) and the SONAR Truckload Volume Index (STVI.USA), as of early November 2026, and on a FreightWaves analysis of the FMCSA Company Census File, snapshot dated November 9, 2026, for the fleet-size distribution and the leased-versus-owned tractor breakdown. Operating-cost and insurance figures are from ATRI’s 2026 Operational Costs of Trucking report. The diesel price is the U.S. Department of Energy on-highway average of 6.127 dollars a gallon for the week of November 9, 2026. Spot and contract rate context reflects published 2026 rate data and forecasts. Census power-unit data is self-reported through MCS-150 filings and includes private and intrastate carriers, and term-leased tractor counts include both owner-operator lease-ons and full-service equipment leases.

Audi Is Making Just 182 Nuvolari Supercars for the U.S. Market, It Asks $700,000 for One
59 photos
Photo: Audi
German carmaker Audi announced this week that it will produce a limited number of the Nuvolari supercar and send just 182 of them to the U.S. in the first half of 2028. On top of being so few of them, there will be so many customization options that they'll likely cause quite the headaches for anyone who has the money and intention to buy one.
The number represents a sizeable chunk of the total of 499 units that are being made for the global market. For North America, the German carmaker announced a starting price of $700,000, not including destination, taxes, title, other options, and dealer charges.
Presented back in early summer, the road-going supercar made its American debut during the Monterey Car Week back in August. It was received with a lot of praise, not only on account of the way it looks, but also because it represents the most powerful and fastest production Audi in history, something that is bound to attract the attention of rich buyers.
The shape of the car, looking like some sort of alien spaceship descended to the ground, owes part of its looks to the carbon fiber bodywork and the active aerodynamics fitted all over, including a three-stage deployable rear wing, a drag-reduction system, and other aerodynamic elements that conspire to generate some 800 pounds (400 kg) of downforce.
Photo: Audi Built around the all-new Audi Space Frame, almost all of the exterior panels that come together to form the Nuvolari are made in carbon fiber, shaped with methods used in Formula 1, just like the DRS mentioned above. And underneath it all hide a number of mechanical solutions that have never before been used by the brand with four rings in this way.
And it all starts with the powertrain, an unforgiving combination between an internal combustion engine and electric motors. A hybrid by trade, the supercar employs a high-revving V8 biturbo engine and three electric axial flux motors (two on the front and one on the rear axle) to develop a combined 987 horsepower (U.S.-spec).
Of that, 789 hp, achieved from 9,000 – 9,750 rpm, come from the ICE, and an extra 198 hp from the electric motors. The troop allows the Nuvolari to hit 60 mph from a perfect standstill in 2.5 seconds, on to a top speed of 217 mph (349 kph).
A new brake-by-wire technology backed by ceramic disks and a series of launch control strategies help the driver harness the immense power levels, while a brand-new, never-before-used quattro predictive ride is on deck to make sure none of that goes to waste.
Photo: Audi The quattro system makes use of data generated by an undisclosed number of sensors to analyze things like grip levels, steering inputs, acceleration, and vehicle behavior, and, based on that, provide the proper torque distribution, braking interventions, and aerodynamic balance. To do that, the system also ties into a four-way adjustable suspension setup.
Audi is sending not only the above to the American market, but also a lot of customization choices that are bound to make every single one of the 182 American examples (and probably the global ones as well) unique in its own way.
For the exterior, for instance, the Germans let people choose from more than 60 colors (50 gloss paints and around 10 matte ones), and match that with one of 13 brake caliper colors. On top of that, there will also be an undisclosed number of Audi Exclusive hues. As a side note, Audi also offers the choice of going for a fully exposed carbon fiber exterior.
Photo: Audi Things don't get easier when it comes to the inside either. Offering just two undisclosed materials to choose from, the Nuvolari throws on the table three primary Dinamica colors and no less than 33 leather color options, a dozen seat belt colors, and a couple of switchgear colors. Finally, the company also talks about fully customized Audi Exclusive paints and interior options, but it does not dive into the details of what that means.
The carmaker is already accepting orders for the insane vehicle, but it only does this at authorized Audi dealerships throughout the country, and it won't do that forever – there is no mention of when the books to reserve a Nuvolari close, but it will probably be soon. As said, deliveries are expected to begin in 2028, which is about one year after the first examples will be delivered to customers in the rest of the world.
Audi sees the extreme ride as a first step to a new direction in car design and engineering, so it's very likely more things such as this will follow in the not-so-distant future. And however these new things will manifest themselves, they will likely be even more extreme, as Audi has already committed to bringing the innovations of Formula 1 to the road in a constant manner.

Alder Is a Popular West Coast Tiny Home That Doesn't Ask You To Give Up Much To Live More Simply
23 photos
Photo: NW Tiny Homes
Some of the biggest misconceptions about tiny homes is that they imply extreme downsizing and that they are primarily meant for nomad living. The truth is there are plenty of larger models that provide residential comfort and are perfectly fitted for full-time stationary living.
With their increased dimensions, residential-style amenities, full-size furniture and appliances, park model tiny homes are great for more permanent small-space living arrangements. The Alder is a good example of how comfortable tiny living can be when there’s enough room for the things that matter.
Offered by NW Tiny Homes, a dealer and builder operating in the Pacific Northwest and offering units built by established manufacturers like Cavco Homes and Champion Park Models & Cabins, the Alder is described as the company’s all-time best-selling model and one of the most popular park model homes on the West Coast.
Some of the things that make it so appealing among people who decide to live full-time in a tiny home are its spacious interior, high ceilings, a spacious kitchen, and its customizable nature. Buyers can personalize various aspects of the design, choosing finishes for cabinetry, countertops, flooring, paint colors, and hardware. Moreover, several exterior siding styles are available, along with optional covered porches, so owners can truly make it feel their own.
Photo: NW Tiny Homes The Alder unit featured here is 35 feet (10.6 meters) long and 11 feet 2 inches (3.4 meters) wide and comes with an 8-foot (2.4-meter) front porch, so it offers a considerably larger footprint compared to a conventional tiny house on wheels.
Aimed at people who are drawn to tiny living but don’t like the idea of extreme downsizing, this park model home boasts a spacious layout that could work for both couples and families, as it includes a commodious downstairs bedroom and a huge loft that can accommodate two twin beds. The rest of the house is dedicated to common living areas and strikes the perfect balance between minimalism and luxury.
Built on a multi-axle trailer and certified to ANSI A119.5 codes, this model is titled as a recreational vehicle, which means it follows RV placement regulations instead of full residential building permits in most areas. Depending on local regulations, owners can place it on private property, in RV parks, or in tiny home communities. It’s also worth mentioning that, given its oversized dimensions, it requires special permits to be towed on public roads and relocated.
Photo: NW Tiny Homes The home’s exterior features four rows of cement lap siding all around, combined with vertical LP SmartPanel. Architectural shingles come standard on the roof, although buyers can upgrade to 16-inch standing seam metal roofing, available in standard and premium colors. Moreover, the Alder is fully insulated and features vinyl-framed, dual-glazed windows.
The most appealing feature on the outside is the covered front porch, which extends the usable living space and creates a comfortable outdoor area perfect for those who love the outdoors and want to live in closer connection with their surroundings.
Like in many conventional brick-and-mortar homes, the front entry door opens directly into a great room rather than a separate hallway or foyer. It combines the living room, kitchen, and dining area in one big, open space that feels inviting and practical. White walls, high ceilings, and several oversized picture windows make this area super luminous. And if you’d rather ditch the built-in porch for an optional deck, you can even have double glass doors for even more natural light and a seamless indoor-outdoor flow.
Photo: NW Tiny Homes Simple yet elegant, the lounge area follows a residential-style arrangement, with a sofa, an entertainment center, and a big flat-screen TV. Next to it is the kitchen with a large peninsula and a separate dining area featuring an elegant round table and chairs.
The kitchen is definitely a highlight of this park model RV , and one of the reasons it has become such a popular tiny living choice. Its U-shaped configuration provides generous cabinetry and countertop space, while the peninsula adds even more work surface for meal prep, while also making the kitchen feel more connected to the lounge.
Photo: NW Tiny Homes The standard cabinetry features Knotty Alder face frames and doors with hidden hinges, and buyers can choose quartz, Corian, or granite countertops. Frigidaire stainless steel appliances, including a gas range, a microwave, a full-size refrigerator, and an 18-inch dishwasher, ensure you get the same functionality as in a conventional house.
The sleeping arrangements are comfortable and cleverly positioned to ensure privacy for all occupants. Downstairs, there is an enclosed, commodious bedroom with a queen-size bed, a wardrobe, and optional wall cabinets above the bed. Above it, a large loft can fit two twin beds, increasing the home’s sleeping capacity.
Unlike the cramped upper sleeping areas found in regular tiny houses , this loft is really spacious, bright, and offers generous headroom. Accessed via easy-to-climb stairs, the loft is carpeted, which gives it more warmth and a traditional bedroom feel.
Photo: NW Tiny Homes Of course, there is also a bathroom inside Alder. Though it’s not very big, it offers all the essentials, including a toilet, a spacious shower cabin, and a vanity with generous counter space, a sink, and a medicine cabinet. A washer/dryer hookup is also included in front of the staircase, adding even more convenience for full-time living.
In terms of pricing, the Alder park model tiny home starts at $67,500, but the company says most buyers end up spending between $72,000 and $85,000, depending on finishes and upgrades. Once an order is confirmed, it takes approximately eight to twelve weeks for the company to complete the build.

Challenger Hellcat Races Shelby GT500 in 1,400-HP Dog Fight in Europe, the Red Fat American Wins
31 photos
Photo: YouTube/Driven+
“A Hellcat and a GT500 duke it out on a track in Europe,” is either the opening line of a great Rodney Dangerfield stand-up show, or a psychological instrument of torture designed by someone with a very twisted sense of humor. “Twisted” is literal here, as in it doesn’t travel straight – which is something neither a Dodge Challenger, nor a Shelby Mustang GT500 were destined for. And yet, here we are, because the internet is always capable of adding an extra layer of zest to a thick, juicy punchline.
American muscle cars have spent the last 60 years perfecting the noble art of treating corners like a personal insult. Europeans have been laughing themselves silly over Detroit's allergy to lateral G-forces since forever, convinced that any machine built west of the Atlantic requires a tugboat license and a prayer to survive a roundabout. Now, a comparative circuit test between two of America's most iconic nameplates will either shatter or cement that stereotype.
The brave souls conducting this scientific experiment are presenter Max Haftavani and professional racing driver Sam Maher-Loughnan from the Driven+ YouTube channel. Instead of a drag strip, they brought two 700-hp American heavyweights to an anti-clockwise British airfield circuit featuring corners that go both left and right, mercifully not at the same time. Before turning a wheel, both men cheerfully agreed that neither machine would travel in a straight line.
Representing Mopar's school of subtle force-fed V8 diplomacy is a 2015 Dodge Challenger SRT Hellcat. The Challenger nameplate debuted in 1969 for the 1970 model year and spanned three generations: the 1970 to 1974 E-body, a forgettable 1978 to 1983 Mitsubishi rebadge, and the third-generation bruiser built from 2008 to 2023. For 2015, Dodge sold 66,365 Challengers, including 7,168 supercharged SRT Hellcat examples in its debut year.
Photo: YouTube/Driven+ This one is among the 869 copies finished in TorRed for 2015, 1 of 3,748 with the TorqueFlite 8-speed automatic gearbox, and 1 of 1,038 wearing 20-inch Brass Monkey forged wheels. Its 6.2-liter supercharged Hemi V8 cranks out 707 hp and 880 Nm of torque (650 lb-ft). Weighing a tectonic 2,045 kg (that’s two full tons) on Continental SportContact 7 tires, this $78,000 leviathan delivers 313.6 hp per ton, 0 to 60 mph in 3.6 seconds, and 199 mph. If the straight is long enough, that is.
Staring down the Dodge is a Race Red Ford Mustang Shelby GT500. The Mustang debuted on April 17, 1964, spanning seven generations by 2026, while Carroll Shelby's GT500 badge arrived in 1967. This car hails from the fifth-generation S197 lineage built between 2005 and 2014, with its GT500 variant running from 2007 to 2014. For 2011, Ford built 68,650 Mustangs and 5,026 GT500s, following 81,024 Mustangs and 4,458 GT500s in 2010.
In standard factory trim, the $49,000 Shelby GT500's 5.4-liter supercharged V8 delivered 540 hp in 2010 and 550 hp in 2011, with 691 Nm of torque (510 lb-ft), 0 to 60 mph in 4.2 seconds, and a 180-mph top speed. Naturally, the owner considered that borderline anemia. Upgraded with headers, a short-throw 6-speed manual, and a tune, his 1.735-ton (3,825-lb) Shelby Mustang GT500 unleashes 700 hp, 818 Nm (603 lb-ft), and 397.4 hp per ton on Goodyear Asymmetric 6 tires.
Photo: YouTube/Driven+ Before unleashing the pair, Sam – a professional racing driver, by the way – argued that wide left-hand-drive American barges excel on British roads because the driver can hug the ditch while using a sacrificial passenger to spot oncoming traffic. He then took the Challenger out in Track mode, returning offended because the computer neutered the throttle. Holding the button for 10 seconds to kill stability control, he warned that doing so usually guarantees a plane crash.
Unchained from electronic supervision, the 2,045-kg (4,500-lb) Hellcat attacked the circuit with the subtlety of a caffeinated grizzly bear crashing a vegan wedding. Its supercharger wailed across the airfield while the rear tires vaporized into white smoke right through the high-speed direction change. Despite a long brake pedal, Sam Maher-Loughnan wrestled the Dodge home in a shockingly rapid 53.51 seconds, awarding it 40 out of a maximum of 50 points.
With the Dodge declared a masterpiece, it was time for the 310-kg (683-lb) lighter Mustang to show how a manual coupe carves up an apex. Firing up the 5.4-liter V8 produced an exhaust detonation so violent, it could easily be misidentified as battleship dress rehearsal for naval warfare. Inside, the racing driver discovered that the driver's seat refused to move an inch, forcing him to brace like a lorry driver while admiring a rifle-bolt white cue-ball shifter.
Photo: YouTube/Driven+ Then came the warm-up lap, where the Shelby's live rear axle decided to file for divorce from the rest of the chassis, physics, and plain common sense in general. Instead of planting its 700 hp evenly, the differential served up a comical one-wheel peel out of every corner while the nose pitched like a trawler. When Sam complained about the body roll, the YouTube host politely revealed that the owner had removed the front anti-roll bar for drag racing. (That was unexpected…)
Armed with a chassis that was actively contorting itself into a pretzel, the brave test driver and arbiter elegantiarum launched the sway-bar-free Shelby into a flying lap that bordered on performance art. Approaching the braking zone, the veteran driver suddenly developed a very spiritual connection to Ford’s brake engineers, begging the calipers and discs to have a consensual relationship – preferably before the GT500 ended wheels up in the grass.
A single-tire smoke screen engulfed the airfield, lingering over the concrete as the tuned Shelby Mustang clocked 55.79 seconds, trailing the heavier Dodge by 2.28 seconds.
Photo: YouTube/Driven+ Climbing out of the mobile smoke machine, Sam immediately embraced his new-found faith, admitting that a single heretic input in the Mustang would have resulted in an immediate meeting with his maker. Even so, the murderous Shelby still earned 10 out of 10 for its engine, 10 for its gearbox, and 10 for sheer fun, alongside a generous 3 for brakes and a brutal 2 for handling, totaling 35 out of 50 points.
So, did this transatlantic showdown silence European track snobs once and for all? In a twist of supreme irony, the fat Dodge Challenger SRT Hellcat proved that an unmodified Detroit bruiser with factory sway bars can hustle around left and right turns without embarrassing Uncle Sam. As for the sway-bar-deleted Mustang, it proved that even when Americans miss a corner, they don’t lose track of their goal. They simply pave a straight-line cloud of tire smoke right to the bullseye.
